feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Project context feeds
feed.subtitle: Real cases from around the world, three times a week, across every Wits AHEAD project.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: Brain pain: Nigerian secondary teachers call relocating abroad a right, but say it still hurts (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A phenomenological study in the Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education interviewed 10 Nigerian secondary teachers individually and ran two focus groups of six public and six private school teachers across five states, to understand why many consider leaving the profession or the country. It coins 'brain pain' for the distress of feeling relocation is a personal right while still fearing harm to students, the loss of STEM teachers, and the devaluation of their credentials abroad; family considerations weighed more than fear of visa rejection or starting over. The author argues that retention policy should address professional dignity and moral distress, not salary alone.

Why it matters here: Mobility schemes like Wits-Aix-Marseille's KA171 project move teacher educators and candidates in both directions rather than only outward, but this study is a caution the project can use directly: outward academic mobility, even short-term, touches the same moral and professional terrain as emigration, and support structures should expect ambivalence and guilt alongside enthusiasm, not treat departure as a simple professional-development decision.

Adamu, C. D., Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A Ghanaian delegation's Erasmus+ KA171 staff week in Berlin opens talks on joint doctoral training (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A five-member delegation from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) took part in an Erasmus+ KA171 staff week at Technische Universität Berlin from 22 to 26 June 2026, alongside six other Sub-Saharan African universities. The week combined sessions on the Africa Charter on Transformative Research Collaborations and on equity and funding in international partnerships with a strategic review of the KNUST-TU Berlin link, including a visit to the Einstein Center Digital Future. Follow-up conversations between a KNUST computer scientist and two TU Berlin professors raised the possibility of fully funded PhD training, a joint course in cloud computing and blockchain, and joint research in federated learning and distributed energy systems.

Why it matters here: A staff week used to negotiate concrete joint courses and co-supervised doctoral training, not only to exchange classroom visits, is a model the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project could borrow for its own staff mobility weeks. It also shows KA171 staff mobility being used elsewhere on the continent to open new doctoral pipelines between an African and a European university, the same ambition behind the Wits-Aix-Marseille link.

KNUST International Programmes Office, 22 July 2026 · Institutional news page from the delegation's own international office, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: Two pilot cohorts, one platform problem: what a gamified introductory computer science track found about motivation over time (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Oslo ran two pilots of a collaborative, game-based learning track alongside an introductory computer science course (42 students, then 73), measuring engagement, motivation and technology comprehension. Reported motivation fell steadily across chapters, from 75 per cent to 42 per cent, and bonus-task engagement dropped sharply once the course moved to an external platform, though satisfaction stayed high (88 to 92 per cent) and gamified-track participants outscored a non-randomised control group on the exam even after controlling for prior grades.

Why it matters here: A cautionary, well-measured case on why a gamified track can lose momentum once the platform changes partway through, directly useful for the Wits team as it plans the platform and pacing of its own semester-long crystallography and phase-transformation sessions.

Mirmotahari, Nordrum Grun and Berg, Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Frontiers in Education), open access

entry.title: A systematic review of fifty studies maps fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics gaps in learning analytics (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A systematic mapping of fifty studies examined how the FATE principles, fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics, are built into learning analytics systems, identifying the tools used, the main ethical and technical challenges, and the stakeholders most affected. The review concludes that ethical practice can support a more equitable use of educational data, and that adopting these systems well requires governance structures and regular audits, with closer attention to the needs of under-represented student populations.

Why it matters here: PASS is itself a predictive model built on anonymised Wits School of Education data, so this review's own FATE checklist, governance, audits and attention to under-represented groups, is a direct test to run against the project's data pipeline and any dashboard, before a model's output reaches the School or its Business Intelligence Services.

Oliveira, Matos, Rodrigues, Lima and Lima, Revista Brasileira de Informática na Educação, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Revista Brasileira de Informática na Educação), systematic literature review

entry.title: A proposed ten-indicator early warning system for Argentina's higher education dropout, built on the OREALC/UNESCO model (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Pointing to Argentina's wide gap between students who enrol, stay and graduate from higher education, this paper designs an early warning system in three stages: identifying dropout risk factors, improving the use of administrative data and management information systems, and defining alert indicators. It sets out ten indicators structured under the Context-Input-Process-Product model used by UNESCO's regional office OREALC, intended to help institutions detect risk early and ground their own intervention strategies, though the paper presents a design rather than a system already evaluated in use.

Why it matters here: The OREALC/UNESCO Context-Input-Process-Product structure behind these ten indicators offers PASS a tested, non-technical frame for organising whatever risk indicators the Wits and Emory model ultimately produces, useful alongside the statistical model itself when the project explains its indicators to the School of Education or its Business Intelligence Services.

Cuttica, Gestión de la Educación, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Gestión de la Educación, Universidad de Costa Rica)

entry.title: More engaged players, higher grades: a gamification case study across first and third-semester engineering courses in León (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
At Tecnológico de Monterrey's León campus, three researchers ran a gamification framework across mathematics, physics and computing courses for 137 first- and third-semester engineering students, with 98 per cent taking part. Students who engaged more fully with the gamified activities averaged a final grade 7.3 per cent higher than less engaged classmates, which the authors link to greater motivation.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable early-semester engineering cohort, with clear participation and grade figures the Wits team can set against its own gamified crystallography and phase-transformation sessions, and a caution that engagement, not gamification alone, is what tracks with the grade gain.

Martinez-Borquez, Mena-Avilés and Mendoza-Gómez, IEEE Global Engineering Education Conference (EDUCON), 2024 · Peer-reviewed IEEE conference proceedings

entry.title: "Safety Hunting": a serious game trains chemical plant workers to spot safety hazards in a short session (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers linked to the Norwegian University of Science and Technology built "Safety Hunting", a serious game that puts chemical plant workers through realistic safety scenarios, and tested it at an international agrochemical production facility in Italy. Players who completed a short session reported improved knowledge of safety procedures and greater confidence, and found the simulated scenarios realistic and engaging. The authors conclude that the learning objectives were met to a satisfactory degree within a short playing time, addressing drawbacks of conventional safety training such as cost and participant immersion.

Why it matters here: This offers the Wits gamification team a concrete example of a short, scenario-based serious game aimed at an industrial, safety-critical setting close to metallurgical and chemical plant practice, a useful contrast to the classroom board games and escape rooms already in this feed.

Tzioutzios, Amati, Baboi and Paltrinieri, Chemical Engineering Transactions, 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings (Chemical Engineering Transactions), open access

entry.title: Wits became a CIVIS strategic partner in Marseille, and a standing Africa-Europe mobility call still runs from it (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
On 15 March 2022, at a conference in Marseille co-hosted by the CIVIS Alliance and Aix-Marseille Université, Wits Vice-Chancellor Professor Zeblon Vilakazi signed Wits on as one of six African strategic partner universities, alongside Makerere, Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, and universities in Casablanca, Sfax and Dakar. That status now runs a standing Erasmus+ International Credit Mobility call, open at any time to Wits and CIVIS faculty, postdoctoral and PhD candidates, and staff, funding stays of five days to six months in both directions.

Why it matters here: Wits already holds a formal, funded route into European mobility through CIVIS, distinct from the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project, and Aix-Marseille Université is itself a CIVIS member and the city where Wits signed. The two schemes can run alongside each other: a KA171 staff member unable to find a slot on the bilateral project could use the standing CIVIS call instead, and the CIVIS Hubs are a ready audience for Wits-Aix-Marseille's own findings on bilingual teacher education.

University of the Witwatersrand, March 2022; CIVIS coordinated mobility call, consulted October 2026 · University's own news report of a signing event, supported by the alliance's own published call

entry.title: An early-alert dashboard tracks every undergraduate's engagement and reaches out by text and email (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of Canterbury's Analytics for Course Engagement (ACE) programme began in early 2020 for first-year students and was extended to all undergraduates in 2021. It combines a student's activity on the LEARN (Moodle) platform and Echo360 lecture recordings into an engagement score, shown to the student on their own dashboard against the course average; when engagement drops during term time the student receives a personalised text message and email, and support teams, including first-year advisors, faculties, Student Accessibility, Halls, Student Care and the Māori and Pasifika Student Support teams, may follow up. The university states that ACE does not track lecture attendance or academic performance and is never used to assess students; the programme won the 2021 CAUDIT award for Improving Student Success.

Why it matters here: ACE is a working example, at full university scale, of the step PASS has not yet reached: turning a predictive signal into a named outreach workflow. Its declared limits, no use of attendance or grades and no assessment of students, are a useful boundary for Wits' Business Intelligence Services to weigh when PASS moves from an anonymised model to contact with real students.

University of Canterbury, Analytics for Course Engagement (ACE) programme · University programme page describing an operating institutional system, not independently peer-reviewed

entry.title: A Kassel materials engineering course has students design their own board, card or digital game about metals (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
The University of Kassel's "Project I: MatWerk GameLab" has small groups of materials engineering students turn phenomena, processes, material properties and key parameters from their coursework into the basis of a board, card or digital game. The module is led by Professor Thomas Niendorf in the Department of Metallic Materials and meets weekly. The course page states that it aims to deepen students' knowledge of materials science and engineering while building teamwork, problem-solving and design skills.

Why it matters here: This is a direct precedent for turning crystallography and phase-transformation content into a student-designed game rather than a ready-made one, close to the co-design workshops the Wits CheMet study plans with its own students. It is a useful contrast to the Wits study's formal evaluation plan, since the Kassel page describes the format but not whether its games are ever formally assessed.

University of Kassel, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, course page (Prof. Dr. Thomas Niendorf) · Official university course page, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A proposed "LEAGUE" framework argues that legal compliance alone cannot make student-data analytics fair or accountable (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Sahana Varadaraju and Bharathwaj Vijayakumar of Rowan University argue that learning-analytics governance in higher education has stayed "compliance-first", centred on meeting baseline legal requirements such as the United States' FERPA and the European Union's GDPR, which they say does not by itself resolve questions of fairness, student agency, accountability or educational purpose. They propose the LEAGUE framework, a six-pillar model (Lawfulness, Equity, Agency, Governance, Utility and Ethics by Design) built from a conceptual synthesis of learning-analytics, educational-data-mining, data-ethics and educational-policy scholarship, and illustrate it with an early-alert case study.

Why it matters here: As PASS moves from building predictive models to co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services, this framework offers a structured checklist, beyond mere compliance with South Africa's POPIA, for whether an early-alert intervention is fair, transparent and respects students' agency, not only whether it is legally permitted.

Varadaraju, S. and Vijayakumar, B., Rowan University, EDULEARN26 Proceedings (IATED), 2026 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (EDULEARN26 proceedings), author manuscript on arXiv, open access

entry.title: A survey experiment finds that a few targeted questions about motivation and degree-completion expectations predict university dropout better than personality measures (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Economists at CNRS and IESEG School of Management (Lille), and at Aarhus University, ran a survey experiment with incoming first-year students, linked to long-run administrative outcomes, to see which information improves dropout prediction beyond standard university records. They found that a small number of targeted, study-specific survey items, especially about motivation and expectations of degree completion, substantially improved predictive performance, while widely used measures of general traits such as grit and self-control added little, a result the authors say they qualitatively replicated in a large population.

Why it matters here: This offers the PASS team a concrete, low-cost addition to test alongside its anonymised Wits School of Education data: a handful of motivation and expectation questions rather than a full personality battery, which the authors report adds little once administrative records are already in the model. It is also a useful caution against assuming established psychological scales will automatically strengthen a predictive model.

Epper, T. F., Ibsen, K., Koch, A. K. and Nafziger, J., IZA Discussion Paper No. 18439, March 2026 · IZA working paper (discussion paper series), not yet peer-reviewed

entry.title: A Graz medical university secures a worldwide Erasmus+ KA171 grant spanning three South African universities and Makerere (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Medical University of Graz's International Office secured EUR 326,063.00 in Erasmus+ KA171 funding for a worldwide mobility project running from August 2025 to July 2028, covering incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility for study, traineeships and teaching and training stays. Its partner universities span 12 countries, including three in South Africa (Cape Town, KwaZulu-Natal and Stellenbosch), Makerere University in Uganda, the University of Namibia, and institutions in Australia, Brazil, Chile, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nepal, Thailand and Ukraine.

Why it matters here: It is a close institutional comparator to the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 grant, showing the scale (over EUR 326,000) and country spread a single global-mobility KA171 project can reach, and a reminder that Wits appears as a partner in other European universities' own KA171 networks, not only as the lead African partner in its own.

Medical University of Graz, International Office, 18 August 2025 · Official university news page, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A 21-institution Erasmus+ virtual exchange trains African and European students and staff to think critically about AI (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
CVEinAI is a 36-month Erasmus+ virtual exchange project, launched in February 2025 and coordinated by the University of Padua, that uses video conferencing, discussion forums and messaging tools to connect students and staff from 21 institutions across 13 countries in Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, Namibia, Ghana and Botswana. It aims to train 50 higher-education staff in Virtual Exchange design, prepare 100 master's and PhD students as online facilitators, and reach 2,400 students with modules on critical thinking about artificial intelligence, ethical and inclusive AI practice, and intercultural collaboration. A pilot course ran in March and April 2026, and the project has already held an awareness webinar with 77 global participants.

Why it matters here: This is a live, AI-focused Erasmus virtual exchange running at a scale the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 partnership has not yet attempted, and it shows what blended or virtual mobility can add alongside physical exchange for teacher educators, including training a cohort of student facilitators rather than relying only on academic staff. Its spread across 13 countries, nearly half of them in Sub-Saharan Africa, is also a useful comparator for how a smaller, bilateral KA171 project like Wits and Aix-Marseille's might grow its own network.

Critical Virtual Exchange in Artificial Intelligence (CVEinAI), coordinated by the University of Padua with Makerere University's College of Education and External Studies, Erasmus+, 2025 to 2028 · Official project page of the lead implementing partner, not peer-reviewed

entry.title: A master's dissertation gamifies organic chemistry laboratory courses at the Federal University of Ceará and measures safety compliance and engagement (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Renner César Silveira Jucá's 201-page master's dissertation at the Federal University of Ceará gamified Experimental Organic Chemistry courses for 100 students in Agronomy, Biotechnology, Pharmacy and Chemistry across three semesters (2023.1, 2023.2 and 2024.1), to address low compliance with safety rules and limited participation in practical sessions. Students earned points, virtual coins, badges and rankings for positive conduct, with a final mark built entirely from accumulated points rather than written tests. A Likert-scale survey found a mean rating of 8.8 out of 10 for the gamified approach and a mean user engagement score of 4.09 out of 5, with more than 80 per cent of students rating each stage of the method positively.

Why it matters here: It offers a directly transferable model for the Wits CheMet study, converting routine laboratory practicals into a points-and-badges system without any written test, and gives a concrete benchmark (8.8 out of 10 engagement, over 80 per cent positive) that the Wits survey and interview instruments could be measured against. Its focus on safety compliance is also relevant to any laboratory-based crystallography or phase-transformation practical the Wits project designs.

Jucá, R. C. S., supervised by da Silva Júnior and Leite Junior, Federal University of Ceará, master's dissertation, 2025 · Master's dissertation in Chemistry, institutional repository (Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations), open access

entry.title: A Stellenbosch study finds South Africa is becoming a confusing "brain circuity" hub for doctoral students from the rest of Africa, not a clean brain drain or brain circulation (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Using national higher education microdata from 2000 to 2019, researchers at Stellenbosch University's Centre for Research on Evaluation, Science and Technology found that doctoral enrolments from the rest of Africa in South African universities rose from 9 per cent of the total in 2000 to 34 per cent in 2019, before levelling off, with four in ten doctoral students in South Africa in 2019 being international and about one in three of those from elsewhere in Africa. A smaller tracking sample of 463 doctoral graduates from the rest of Africa found 27.5 per cent remained in South Africa, 63.8 per cent returned to their home countries on the continent, and 5.0 per cent moved on to other countries. The authors argue that neither the brain drain nor the brain circulation theory fits cleanly, and coin "brain circuity" for a flow of knowledge marked by indirection and unresolved tension between equity for the rest of Africa and South Africa's own doctoral development targets.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, data-grounded caution for any Africa-Europe mobility scheme that assumes doctoral and staff movement simply flows back to benefit the sending country: the Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 project and the CIVIS alliance should expect the same mix of return, onward movement and continued stay that this study finds for South Africa itself, rather than a simple two-way exchange.

Van Schalkwyk, F. B., Van Lill, M. H. and Cloete, N., South African Journal of Science, 2021 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A randomised Dutch field experiment finds that an accurate early-warning system did not, by itself, reduce first-year dropout (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam ran a randomised field experiment at a large Dutch university to test whether an early-warning system, used by student counsellors to flag at-risk students for early intervention, reduced first-year dropout. The early-warning system accurately predicted which students were at risk, but the counselling it triggered did not reduce dropout or improve academic performance. The authors suggest that addressing poor academic performance may need more actionable feedback and better-targeted counselling practices than the warning alone provided.

Why it matters here: This is the clearest caution available to the PASS team that an accurate predictive model is not enough on its own: identifying at-risk Wits School of Education students correctly will not improve their outcomes unless the interventions that follow are themselves effective, a question PASS's co-creation work with the University's Business Intelligence Services will need to test directly rather than assume.

Plak, S., Cornelisz, I., Meeter, M. and van Klaveren, C., Higher Education Quarterly, 2022 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A Monterrey study of a semester-long engineering game finds higher grades for active players, but only for those who chose to take part (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Jenny Díaz-Ramírez ran an optional, semester-long gamified system alongside two groups of an operations research engineering course at Universidad de Monterrey in autumn 2019, coordinated through a WhatsApp group and awarding points, badges and tradeable benefits for mastery, institutional and teamwork activities. Of 56 students who joined, 59 per cent were classed as active; active players had higher average grades in both groups, and in one group every student who failed was non-active. An end-of-semester survey found that about 90 per cent of active players believed the game improved their learning.

Why it matters here: Its own limitation is the useful lesson here: because participation was self-selected rather than randomly assigned, higher grades among active players show association, not proof that the game caused the improvement, a caution the Wits CheMet team should build into how it interprets its own surveys, interviews and classroom observation. The WhatsApp-based points-and-badges mechanic is also a low-cost model the team could trial.

Díaz-Ramírez, J., Universidad de Monterrey, Heliyon, 2020 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A Barcelona chemistry thesis designs materials science lab games for metallography and steel heat treatments, but admits they were never piloted (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Clara Molina Perpinyà's final-year chemistry thesis at the University of Barcelona set out to close a gap she identified between students' strong scores on end-of-session quizzes and their weaker results in the final Materials Science exam. Using a Design Thinking process and a student survey that found low participation and limited autonomy, she designed quizzes, puzzles, memory games, role-play and prediction challenges for five laboratory practicals, including heat treatments of steels and metallography. The thesis states that the proposal could not be implemented or experimentally validated, and recommends future pilot studies.

Why it matters here: The thesis targets almost the same gap the Wits CheMet study is testing, a mismatch between in-session success and real exam performance in crystallography-adjacent topics such as heat treatments of steels and metallography, and proposes comparable light-touch games for the same content. Its candid admission that the games were never piloted is a useful caution for the Wits team to build evaluation into its surveys, interviews and classroom observation from the outset.

Molina Perpinyà, supervised by Martínez López and Díaz-Marcos, Universitat de Barcelona, bachelor's thesis, 2026 · University of Barcelona bachelor's thesis (Treball Final de Grau), institutional repository, open access

entry.title: Simplest model wins: comparing four algorithms for predicting student attrition at a Kenyan university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A study at the Technical University of Mombasa compared Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forest and Naive Bayes for predicting student attrition from a Kenyan university dataset gathered through a student questionnaire, using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and ROC-AUC as evaluation criteria. Logistic Regression performed best, reaching 56.67% accuracy and a ROC-AUC of 0.60, while Decision Trees and Random Forest each started at 40% accuracy, with Random Forest improving to 52% after hyperparameter tuning, and Naive Bayes reached 46.67% accuracy with a balanced F1 score of 0.47.

Why it matters here: The study is a useful methodological comparison for PASS because it tests the same shortlist of classical algorithms, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Decision Trees and Naive Bayes, on a Kenyan university's own student data rather than an imported dataset, and finds that the simplest model can still outperform ensemble methods when a dataset is modest in size. Its modest accuracy scores are also a reminder that PASS should expect, and report honestly, model performance that may fall well short of figures obtained on larger or more established datasets until the Wits School of Education's own records grow.

Nyawira, Musau, Adem and Jobunga, Journal of the Kenya National Commission for UNESCO, 2025 · Academic journal article (Journal of the Kenya National Commission for UNESCO), open access

entry.title: An Erasmus+ Teacher Academy building an AI translation tool for multilingual primary classrooms (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt coordinates the SmartStart Erasmus+ Teacher Academy, a three-year project announced in December 2024 that brings together twelve partner institutions across Germany, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Sweden, Slovakia and Spain with just under 1.5 million euros from the Erasmus+ Teacher Academies initiative. The programme trains teachers and student teachers to use AI-based tools in elementary classrooms through an online course on the eTwinning platform followed by practical work in partner schools, and it is developing a dedicated AI translation tool meant to help integrate children who start school with limited language skills and to let the project's own experts, who speak different languages, exchange expertise.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille mobility already pairs virtual and blended preparation with physical exchange for bilingual teaching students; this consortium's purpose-built AI translation tool, designed to bridge language gaps in multilingual classrooms and among multilingual project staff, is a concrete piece of technology the partnership could test for its own bilingual teacher training.

Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, news release, 2024 · Institutional news release (Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt)

entry.title: MineLearn: a Swedish university and mining companies build one gamified simulation of the whole mining value chain (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
MineLearn is a project at Luleå University of Technology in Sweden that ran from November 2024 to June 2025 with the mining companies Boliden and Viscaria, to build a gamified learning platform simulating key components of the mining value chain. The platform integrates Environmental, Social and Governance principles and aims to build technical knowledge among future mining professionals while promoting sustainable and socially responsible practice. It is funded through the Impact Innovation programme for Swedish Metals and Minerals, run jointly by the Swedish Energy Agency, Formas and Vinnova, with a prototype evaluated by experts and a report on scaling it up as planned outputs.

Why it matters here: MineLearn shows what a funded university-industry partnership can build when it gamifies an entire value chain rather than a single topic, a useful scale and partnership contrast for the Wits CheMet team as it weighs its own course-based board and digital games on crystallography and phase transformations. It is also a reminder to consider a sustainability framing alongside the technical content.

Luleå University of Technology, MineLearn project page, 2024-2025 · University project page (Luleå University of Technology), part of a government-funded innovation programme

entry.title: A Malaysian systematic review of 22 studies on game-based learning across engineering education (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three researchers in the Department of Engineering Education at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia carried out a systematic review of game-based learning in engineering education, searching IEEE Xplore and screening records with the Rayyan AI tool before including 22 studies published between January 2019 and April 2024. The review covered simulations, virtual reality, serious games, and digital and non-digital board games, and found that game-based learning was used mostly at undergraduate level, most often in fields linked to digital technology, with reported gains in engagement, motivation, knowledge acquisition and practical skills.

Why it matters here: This review's list of 22 studies and the design features it identifies, interactive gameplay, feedback mechanisms and simulated environments, gives the Wits CheMet team a benchmark of what has already been shown to work across engineering disciplines before it reports its own findings on board games and digital games for crystallography and phase transformations.

Raja Rosli, Techanamurthy and Zakaria, ASEAN Journal of Engineering Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (ASEAN Journal of Engineering Education), open access

entry.title: Ten Chinese doctoral students in Malaysia show how South-South mobility can still reproduce Western academic dominance (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Based on qualitative interviews with ten Chinese doctoral students about their perceptions of studying in Malaysia, researchers including Ly Thi Tran at Deakin University examined global South-South student mobility through a decolonization and recolonization framework. They found that students drew real benefits from this alternative route and used it to question Western academic supremacy, but that their own coping strategies and self-perceptions often ended up reinforcing Western dominance rather than displacing it, producing feelings of positivity and inclusion alongside inferiority and anxiety all at once. The authors call for closer attention to the subtler inequalities that persist within mobility routes that bypass the traditional Global South to Global North pattern.

Why it matters here: The Wits-Aix-Marseille mobility runs the conventional South-North route that this article contrasts with South-South alternatives; its finding that moving outside the usual route does not automatically escape Western academic hierarchies is a caution for how the partnership frames its own candidates' time in France: success should be judged by what candidates gain, not simply by the fact that they travelled to Europe.

Xu, Tran & Xie, Higher Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Higher Education, Springer)

entry.title: No evidence dashboards lift grades: a systematic review of 38 learning-analytics studies (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A systematic and quantitative review of 38 research studies on learning analytics dashboards found no evidence to support the claim that they have improved students' academic achievement, with most individual studies reporting negligible or small effects and few well-powered controlled experiments among them. The review found a relatively substantial effect of dashboards on student participation, with several studies reporting medium to large effect sizes, but only modest and inconsistent effects on motivation and attitudes, and it identified recurring weaknesses such as comparing dashboard users with non-users instead of randomising, assuming that access equates to use, and a lack of standardised outcome measures.

Why it matters here: This review is a direct caution for PASS: a model that correctly flags at-risk students will not by itself raise achievement unless the dashboard built on it, and the interventions that follow, are evaluated with a properly controlled design rather than by simply comparing students who engage with it to those who do not. Before Emory and Wits report any effect of a PASS dashboard to the Wits School of Education or its Business Intelligence Services, the review's own list of recurring design weaknesses is a checklist worth testing the evaluation against.

Kaliisa, Misiejuk, López-Pernas, Khalil and Saqr, LAK '24 (ACM), 2024 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (ACM Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK '24), Best Full Paper award

entry.title: What a national dataset of 21,000 Mexican academics shows about who still controls South-North academic mobility (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Drawing on an anonymised national dataset of the 21,257 academics and scientists registered with Mexico's Sistema Nacional de Investigadores and qualified to doctoral level in 2013, researchers based at the Institut de recherche pour le développement and the University of East Anglia found that nearly 40 per cent had obtained part or all of their qualifications abroad. Seventy per cent of those seeking international qualifications went to the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, and to a lesser extent Germany and Canada, countries that have held this top position for four decades, while Latin America took in 6 per cent of the sample with no single country standing out, and Asia, Northern Europe, Oceania and Africa, including South Africa, together attracted only 3 per cent. The authors conclude that these study trajectories, while gradually diversifying, keep consolidating a small number of host countries at the top of the global higher education field.

Why it matters here: This large-scale national dataset is a sobering check on how far one Erasmus+ KA171 partnership can shift an established pattern: it shows that new South-North academic ties, however welcome, tend to keep reinforcing the same handful of dominant destinations, so the Aix-Marseille-Wits project should track whether its own mobility genuinely widens Wits candidates' options or simply adds one more well-trodden route to Europe.

Gérard & Lebeau, International Journal of Educational Development, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Educational Development), open access

entry.title: Weak at enrolment, strong after first grades: predicting dropout risk across eight Chilean universities (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Drawing on data from eight Chilean universities, the study found that information available at the point of matriculation only weakly predicted whether a student would persist, while the model's predictive power improved markedly once first university grades became available. Financial aid predicted higher persistence and being denied a student's first-choice major predicted lower persistence, and the authors found that student success programmes were effective at some universities and ineffective at others, often failing even where effective to reach the highest-risk students.

Why it matters here: This is a close precedent for PASS's own staged approach, since it shows that a predictive model's power grows chiefly once in-programme performance data, not just admissions data, becomes available, so PASS should expect its earliest Wits School of Education models to sharpen after a first semester or year of local grades. It is also a caution that identifying at-risk students is not enough on its own: PASS's interventions, co-created with the University's Business Intelligence Services, will need checking that they reach the highest-risk students and not only the easiest to help.

Von Hippel and Hofflinger, Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, 2021 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, Taylor & Francis)

entry.title: Guanxi and the dual-teacher model as predictors: a hybrid Random Forest-Neural Network framework for Chinese student retention (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at City University, Malaysia propose a hybrid Random Forest-Neural Network model for predicting dropout and delayed graduation in Chinese undergraduate populations, combining demographic, academic, financial, psychological and institutional data with feature engineering and data-balancing methods. The authors report that academic failure, financial hardship, mental health problems and practical difficulties are the strongest predictors, and argue that adding culturally specific constructs, guanxi (social-network obligation), Confucian pedagogical structures and the dual-teacher model, improved how well the model fits Chinese higher-education settings.

Why it matters here: The paper is a reminder that a predictive model built on one country's assumptions about what predicts dropout may miss locally specific factors; before PASS extends beyond the Wits School of Education, the Emory-Wits team should ask what comparably specific South African or Global South constructs, language of instruction, extended-family financial obligation, distance from home, its own model may be missing.

Zhang and Chamran, International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences), open access

entry.title: A narrative tabletop game for the organic chemistry lab lifts marks across two cohorts in Lisbon (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at two Lisbon institutions built a narrative tabletop game around an "identification of an unknown" laboratory challenge, in which students earned in-game currency by solving chemistry problems and completing laboratory tasks, then spent it on analytical data such as infrared spectra and elemental analysis. Comparing one cohort of 126 students who played the game with two prior, non-gamified years, the practical mean grade rose by 0.56 points (p = 0.02) and the theoretical mean by 0.37 points (p = 0.045); a survey with a 46% response rate reported perceived gains in motivation and understanding, though some students found managing the in-game resources difficult.

Why it matters here: This is one of the few gamification studies in the feed with a measured grade effect and an effect size alongside the usual motivation survey, a model the Wits team can borrow directly for testing whether gamified crystallography sessions move marks, not just enthusiasm, against the two or three years of ungamified cohorts it already has on file.

Crucho, Gomes and Avó, Chemistry Teacher International, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Chemistry Teacher International), open access

entry.title: Twenty-one Italian universities, seventy-eight African partners: Brescia's recovery-funded doctoral and staff mobility scheme (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Università degli Studi di Brescia coordinates TNE UNITAFRICA, a transnational education scheme joining 21 Italian universities, through the Coordinamento Universitario per la Cooperazione allo Sviluppo, with 78 partner institutions across Africa, funded through Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan rather than Erasmus+. Its 2025 call funded three doctoral mobilities of two months each and three staff teaching mobilities of eight days each, to be hosted at one of ten named partner universities in Senegal, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, Somalia and Mozambique, in agriculture, architecture, engineering and global health.

Why it matters here: A national recovery fund, rather than Erasmus+, paying for short, tightly scoped doctoral and staff mobilities to a fixed list of named partner universities is a workable alternative funding model and administrative shape the Aix-Marseille-Wits project can point to if Erasmus+ KA171 funding for this partnership is ever interrupted or needs a smaller, faster-to-run complement.

Università degli Studi di Brescia, international mobility notice, 2025 · Institutional notice (Università degli Studi di Brescia)

entry.title: Nine in ten staff say their professional network grew, but two in three call their institution's recognition merely "informal" (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
France's national Erasmus+ agency tracked 7,142 staff members, 42% of them from higher education, who took part in Erasmus+ mobility in 2016/17, through participant feedback and a follow-up survey sent eighteen months after their mobility ended. Ninety-one per cent said the experience had boosted or strengthened their professional network, half said they had actively or moderately changed their professional practice as a result, and two-thirds said their institution had recognised the value of their mobility, but mostly only informally rather than through any formal process.

Why it matters here: The gap this report finds between personal gains and institutional recognition is exactly the risk for the Aix-Marseille-Wits exchange: unless returning staff and academics have a formal route, a seminar series, a curriculum review, a credited role, to carry what they learned back into the Wits School of Education's own teaching, the mobility risks staying a personal benefit rather than becoming an institutional one.

Agence Erasmus+ France / Éducation Formation, The Erasmus+ Observatory, Notes No. 12, 2025 · National agency evaluation report (Agence Erasmus+ France / Éducation Formation), survey-based

entry.title: Dominoes, bingo and hangman for the economics of chemical plants: five games for a Master's course in Granada (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Granada built five gamified activities, dominoes, bingo, a word search, hangman and a "pass the word" game, for the economic analysis block of a Master's course in chemical product and process design, and ran them across three academic years. Students who took part reported improved motivation, participation and learning, together with a more positive view of collaboration and teamwork than in earlier, non-gamified years of the same block.

Why it matters here: The project ran five different light-touch games inside one difficult, calculation-heavy topic rather than building one elaborate simulation, a template the Wits team can test cheaply against its own gamified sessions on crystallography and phase transformations before committing to a single larger game.

Martín-Lara, Altmajer, Vicaria Rivillas and Muñoz-Batista, Education for Chemical Engineers, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Education for Chemical Engineers), open access

entry.title: Six warnings for virtual exchange as it moves from language classrooms to the Global South (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A University of León researcher traces how virtual exchange has grown from early bilingual North-North language partnerships into North-South collaborations and partnerships with conflict zones, and sets out six concerns for practitioners: structural inequalities in project design that risk reproducing Global North dominance, communication barriers in lingua franca exchanges that favour already-privileged learners, psychological risks for students paired with conflict-zone partners, political and institutional pressure around controversial partnerships, the gap between genuine social impact and tokenistic engagement, and keeping motivated an increasingly well-travelled student population. The author calls for virtual exchange programmes that address power imbalances directly, give stronger linguistic scaffolding and use trauma-informed protocols rather than treating any cross-border contact as automatically beneficial.

Why it matters here: Erasmus+ KA171 moves people rather than running virtual exchanges, but the Aix-Marseille-Wits mobility runs alongside blended and virtual preparation in both directions; this is a direct checklist against which to test whether the project's own design, who sets the agenda, whose language dominates, what happens to the partnership if either side's politics shift, avoids reproducing the imbalance the article warns against.

O'Dowd, Language Learning & Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Language Learning & Technology), open access

entry.title: Gamit!: a shared gamification platform two Latin American universities built for engineering courses (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Universidad de Lima (Peru) and Tecnológico de Monterrey (Mexico) jointly built Gamit!, a gamification platform meant to raise engagement, improve students' attitudes to learning and ease the workload of teaching staff. The two universities trialled it for five weeks in a Modelling of Movement in Engineering course, studying it qualitatively across four dimensions: attention, engagement, resilience and usability, as a continuation of the teams' earlier gamification work together.

Why it matters here: A platform shared across two universities, rather than one bespoke classroom game, is a reminder that the Wits and partner teams could design their crystallography and phase-transformation games as a reusable tool from the outset, so that other engineering courses at Wits, or other institutions, can adopt the same build rather than starting again.

Rincón-Flores, Santos-Guevara, Rodríguez Rodríguez, Martínez-Cardiel, Matsuura Sonoda and Quintana Cruz, IEEE EDUCON 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (IEEE Global Engineering Education Conference, EDUCON 2023)

entry.title: Built for a Ghanaian university, tested on open data: a PhD thesis reaches 92% accuracy on which students will not graduate (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A PhD thesis at South Africa's Durban University of Technology set out to predict which students at a Ghanaian higher education institution were at risk of not graduating, combining activity logs, course and demographic data and assessment records; in the absence of the Ghanaian institution's own data, the model was built and tested on the UK's Open University Learning Analytics Dataset. A Random Forest model outperformed gradient boosting, CatBoost, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and naive Bayes on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score, and when trained only on the most useful features, assignment submission date, total clicks on learning activities, assessment score, registration date, credits studied and unregistration date, it reached 92% accuracy in less time than a model using every available feature.

Why it matters here: The thesis is a direct precedent for PASS's own plan to validate a predictive model on one dataset before it has enough local records: PASS can test the same shortlist of high-value features, submission timing, activity clicks, assessment scores, against its own Wits School of Education data once available, rather than waiting to build a full feature set first.

Tahiru, PhD thesis, Durban University of Technology, 2023 · PhD thesis (Durban University of Technology, Information Technology), institutional repository

entry.title: StudentAnalyse at Prague's Czech Technical University: first-year dropout nearly halved after a four-year early-warning rollout (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The Open University's OU Analyse predictive learning analytics research was adapted as StudentAnalyse for the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering at the Czech Technical University in Prague, which had a first-year drop-out rate averaging 37% before adopting it in 2015/16. Tutors used the system to flag at-risk students and apply intervention strategies; across the following four academic years, to 2018/19, the average drop-out rate fell to 19%, 422 more students progressed to second and third year, and the Vice-Dean reported about CZK 27.9 million (roughly GBP 950,000) in additional tuition income over that period.

Why it matters here: A single, tutor-facing risk dashboard sustained over several years, not a one-off model, is what took this faculty's drop-out rate down by half; it is the kind of multi-year institutional commitment PASS will need from the Wits School of Education's own Business Intelligence Services if an early model is to become a lasting intervention rather than a one-off pilot.

The Open University, Computing Research impact case study, "Using predictive learning analytics to improve student retention" · Institutional impact case study (The Open University), self-reported by the partner institutions

entry.title: Warning emails to students flagged as likely to drop out: no average effect at a German university, and responses that depend on who receives them (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Economists from the University of Wuppertal, the RWI Leibniz Institute for Economic Research and RH Köln evaluated a low-cost early alert system at a German university that emailed warnings to students whose predicted dropout probability was high. The average effect of the warnings was not statistically significant, but responses differed: previously active students, especially outside STEM, cut their exam registrations by up to two courses and modestly improved their grades, while inactive students did not respond and dropout probability rose slightly in structured programmes. The authors used causal forests to examine this variation and conclude that warnings must fit students' prior engagement, the structure of their programme and the timing of the intervention.

Why it matters here: This is the caution PASS needs before it hands risk scores to Wits: an accurate prediction does not by itself change outcomes, and a bare warning can even backfire for some students. Interventions co-created with Business Intelligence Services should therefore be tested for who responds, not only whether the average improves, and timed to the Wits School of Education's own programme structure.

Berens, Henao, Rumert and Schneider, Education Economics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, published online ahead of issue (Taylor and Francis)

entry.title: Ireland tracks every new undergraduate through one national student record, and publishes progression and completion as an open dashboard (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Ireland's Higher Education Authority (HEA) reports progression, continuation and completion for full-time undergraduate new entrants at the institutions it funds, using the national Student Record System census that institutions return each 1 March, and publishes the results as an interactive dashboard that can be filtered by institution and field of study. Its 2026 release finds that 9.3% of 2023/24 new entrants neither progressed nor transferred to another institution, the lowest rate since 2019/20, ranging from 4.5% in Education to 18.8% in Services, with mature entrants at 13.4%. Of students who entered in 2019/20, 76.6% had completed a programme by 2024, with Education highest at 90.4%.

Why it matters here: The HEA dashboard shows what a shared, institution-level evidence base for progression looks like, with small cells suppressed to protect students, and its Education figures give PASS an outside benchmark for the Wits School of Education. Business Intelligence Services at Wits could adopt the same clear definitions of progressed, transferred and non-progressed students before any predictive model is trained.

Higher Education Authority, Ireland, news release by James Holohan, 9 July 2026 · Official national statistics from Ireland's higher education funding and policy agency

entry.title: Teach4Sustainability: an Erasmus+ virtual exchange links student teachers in four African countries with peers in Germany and Spain (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Teach4Sustainability is an Erasmus+ Virtual Exchange project of 36 months, running from February 2026 to January 2029, that connects student teachers, teacher educators and institutions in Germany, Spain, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Rwanda and The Gambia to strengthen climate change and sustainability education in teacher training. Coordinated by Universität Münster, it works through small intercultural groups, real-time and flexible online interaction and problem-based learning, in formats designed to be mobile-friendly and accessible in low-bandwidth settings. The consortium held its first virtual kick-off meeting in February 2026 and launched a multi-country needs assessment in April 2026.

Why it matters here: Not every Wits or Aix-Marseille student teacher will travel, so this is a ready model for the virtual side of the KA171 exchange: structured online work between African and European student teachers on sustainable development, one of the joint themes named in the project. Its design for phones and low bandwidth is a practical lesson for any joint sessions that include Wits School of Education students.

Institut für Didaktik der Geographie, Universität Münster, project page, 2026 · Official project page of the coordinating university (Universität Münster), for a project funded under the Erasmus+ Virtual Exchanges call for Sub-Saharan Africa (ERASMUS-EDU-2025-VIRT-EXCH-SSA, project 101251923); partners and dates also confirmed on the UNED project page and in Münster's launch notice of 30 January 2026

entry.title: Predicting dropout across Saudi universities from 4,560 students, with work, family and cultural factors alongside grades (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers built dropout prediction models for Saudi universities that go beyond academic records to include personal, social and cultural factors, noting that national reports put non-completion among Saudi university students at 40% to 50% while few studies had looked across several institutions. Using data from 4,560 students and twelve feature-selection-based learning models, they found that a K-Nearest Neighbors model with Recursive Feature Elimination performed best, with an accuracy of 97.6%. SHAP and LIME explanations identified GPA, academic year, employment status, support from family and friends and prior knowledge of the major as the most influential features, and a formal evaluation framework found that LIME's explanations outperformed SHAP's on fidelity, local concordance, prescriptivity and stability.

Why it matters here: PASS can borrow the study's two-layer design: registry variables such as GPA and year of study, which Business Intelligence Services already hold for the Wits School of Education, plus survey items on employment and family support that registry data miss. Its near-perfect accuracy on a single dataset is also a reminder that PASS should validate its models on later cohorts before any model guides an intervention.

Albugami, Wali and Almagrabi, PeerJ Computer Science, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Challenges in the maths class: a quasi-experiment on gamification and motivation among engineering students in Lima (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers from three Peruvian universities tested challenge-based gamification with 120 engineering students taking a basic mathematics for engineers course in Lima. In a quasi-experimental design with a control group and an experimental group, an observation rubric and a motivation questionnaire were applied before and after the intervention. The experimental group showed significantly higher academic motivation afterwards, including interest in learning, perseverance and effort, and the value students placed on their tasks.

Why it matters here: The design offers a ready template for the pre and post measures planned in the Wits study, but it is also a caution: the outcome is self-reported motivation rather than learning, and on one motivation dimension the two groups already differed before the intervention. The Wits team can borrow the challenge format while pairing it with concept tests on crystallography and phase transformations, so that gains in enthusiasm are not mistaken for gains in understanding.

Anticona-Valderrama, Risco Sernaque and Serna-Landivar, LACCEI LEIRD 2025 Proceedings, 2025 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (LACCEI LEIRD 2025), open access, full text in Spanish with English abstract

entry.title: Why Ghanaian graduates of European universities go home or stay: 45 interviews on the return decision (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Charles University interviewed 45 Ghanaians who had graduated from European universities: 22 returnees interviewed in Ghana and 23 non-returnees interviewed abroad. Combining the Theory of Planned Behaviour with migration concepts, they found that return intentions often shift over time and that the decision is rarely driven by a single factor, but by an interplay of structural constraints, personal motivations and normative pressures. Participants expressed both pro-return and pro-stay orientations, yet perceived family expectations tended to favour staying abroad.

Why it matters here: KA171 stays are short and return is built in, but this study shows that intentions to stay can grow after a European experience, so the Wits School of Education should plan how returning master's and doctoral candidates are drawn back into its work rather than assume it. It also gives the project a frame for asking what the sending institution gains from the exchange with Aix-Marseille, not only how many people travel.

Yeboah, M., & Novotný, J., International Journal of Educational Development, 2025 · Peer-reviewed article, International Journal of Educational Development (Elsevier), a qualitative interview study by researchers at Charles University

entry.title: Bronze, silver and gold: a points-and-medals scheme across civil engineering courses at United Arab Emirates University (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Civil engineering lecturers at United Arab Emirates University ran a structured bonus-point system across several courses, with class sizes from 17 to 71 students, rewarding completed tasks, good assignment results and attendance. Point totals earned bronze, silver or gold medals, and students who met point and attendance thresholds won a grand prize of a 3% boost to the course grade. The authors report that initial feedback showed higher motivation and enthusiasm, and the same team has since outlined a planned follow-up comparing a hands-on game with an AI-enhanced virtual game across four civil engineering disciplines.

Why it matters here: This is a low-cost, course-level model that a Wits metallurgy module could pilot quickly, and tiered medals are easy to explain to students. It also raises a question the Wits study should test rather than assume: whether rewards tied to marks and attendance deepen understanding of structure-property relationships or simply buy participation, and the planned AI-enhanced version offers a useful comparison for the project's interest in AI-mediated games.

Bediwy, Issa, Abdelsamie and Masoud, EDULEARN25 Proceedings (IATED), 2025 · Conference proceedings paper (EDULEARN25, IATED), abstract freely available, full text restricted

entry.title: A 3D phone game for workshop safety: mechanical engineering students in Indonesia learn to spot hazards in a virtual machining workshop (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A team led from Universitas Negeri Padang built an Android game in Unity 3D that recreates a machining workshop: students steer 3D avatars through hazardous situations, with points, levels, achievements, challenges and rewards, and prompts to follow occupational health and safety rules such as wearing helmets and gloves. Developed through the 4D model (define, design, develop, disseminate) with 64 mechanical engineering students, the app was rated very valid by subject and media experts and very practical by lecturers and students. In a one-group pre-test and post-test with 30 students, mean scores rose from about 51 to 83, which the authors classify as an effective normalised gain.

Why it matters here: Metallurgical engineering students also learn in laboratories and workshops where furnaces, molten metal and machining carry real risk, so a phone-based safety simulation of this kind is a practical kit idea to sit alongside games on crystallography and phase transformations. The study also shows the limits of a one-group design with no comparison class, which the Wits team can avoid by planning a comparison group from the start.

Fortuna, Prasetya, Samala, Nabawi and colleagues, International Journal of Information and Education Technology, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Four universities in Finland and Mozambique co-create teacher education modules and train 912 educators and teachers (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The TEPATE project, run from 2020 to 2024 and funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Finland, joined the Pedagogical University of Maputo and ISET One World in Mozambique with Jamk University of Applied Sciences and the University of Lapland to improve the balance between theory and practice in Mozambican teacher education. Across the 4 universities, 36 teacher educators developed 3 modules for teacher education, 276 student teachers piloted them, and 912 teacher educators, secondary school teachers and school managers were trained on their content. The project lists weak multilingualism pedagogies among the problems facing the teaching profession that it set out to address.

Why it matters here: This is a worked model of what the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership can aim for beyond individual trips: teacher educators from both sides co-creating modules, piloting them with student teachers and carrying them into schools. Its attention to multilingualism pedagogies speaks directly to the bilingual teaching master's at the heart of the exchange with INSPE.

Jamk University of Applied Sciences news, 2024 · University news article, institutional source (Jamk University of Applied Sciences, a project partner), reporting the results of a project funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Finland

entry.title: Graded by the tower they build: a game-based assessment of civil engineering graduate attributes for accreditation at a Costa Rican university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Costa Rica's Civil Engineering School designed a tower-construction game-based assessment and ran it at three curricular stages (initial, intermediate and advanced) in the degree programme. Observable performance indicators from 28 student teams, more than 110 students in all, were normalised to 0-100 scores covering five graduate attributes: design and development, environment and sustainability, teamwork, problem analysis, and project administration and finances. Design and development, environment and sustainability, and teamwork improved significantly across the three stages, problem analysis stayed stable, and a student survey found high clarity and fairness.

Why it matters here: This is a rare case of gamified assessment used for formal programme-level accreditation evidence rather than for teaching alone, which speaks directly to the diversified-assessment strand of the Wits study: a hands-on building task scored against named graduate attributes could be adapted to generate comparable evidence of what students actually grasp about structure-property relationships, alongside the surveys and classroom observation already planned.

Mata Abdelnour, Cruz-Zuñiga and Centeno Mora, Quality Assurance in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, ahead of print, subscription access (Emerald Publishing)

entry.title: AI turns calculus review sheets into arcade-style games for engineering students at a Guatemalan university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Engineering lecturers at Universidad Galileo in Guatemala used AI tools to turn conventional calculus review worksheets into 'Fun Study Guides': browser-based, HTML5 game prototypes with timers, score counters and ranking tables. Three prototypes are described, Multivariable Calculus: Arcade Challenge, Integral Invaders and Quantico: Numerical Mission, covering multivariable calculus and numerical methods such as root finding, interpolation and numerical integration. The paper, presented at the 2026 ASEE Annual Conference in Charlotte, sets out the design and build process but reports no student evaluation data yet.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, low-cost template for the 'AI-generated or AI-mediated games' strand named in the Wits project brief: lecturers, not programmers, used AI tools to convert their own existing worksheets into games, which is exactly the kind of co-design the Wits study's workshops could test for turning crystallography or phase-transformation problem sheets into quick digital games.

Cotto, Alvarado and Portillo, 2026 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper (ASEE Annual Conference proceedings), open access via the ASEE PEER repository

entry.title: An Erasmus+ project trains 40 lecturers across five African countries to lead teacher education for sustainable development (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Leuphana Universität Lüneburg leads an Erasmus+ capacity-building project on teacher leadership for education for sustainable development, working with universities in South Africa, Zambia, Namibia, Malawi and Kenya alongside partners in Germany, Cyprus and Greece. By May 2026 the project had completed a Training of Trainers programme producing 40 trained lecturers able to teach education for sustainable development leadership courses and guide colleagues in running education for sustainable development change projects. The University of the Witwatersrand leads the scaling of these change projects jointly with the University of Malawi.

Why it matters here: The University of the Witwatersrand already runs an international Erasmus+ consortium role here, leading change-project scaling jointly with the University of Malawi, so the Wits School of Education can draw directly on its own cascade model, the Training of Trainers approach that turned 40 lecturers into in-house trainers, when preparing staff and candidates for the Aix-Marseille exchange.

Hülsmann, M., Leuphana Universität Lüneburg news, 2026 · University news article, institutional source (Leuphana Universität Lüneburg), reporting on an active Erasmus+-funded capacity-building project

entry.title: University of Sharjah builds an explainable dropout early-warning system from a decade of UAE STEM enrolment records (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Sharjah built an explainable machine-learning early-warning system to flag dropout risk among undergraduate STEM students in the MENA region, using longitudinal data from 6,798 students at a major UAE university spanning ten cohorts from 2010 to 2019. Of six classifiers tested on routine student information system records, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting Machine and Random Forest performed best, each reaching an AUC-ROC above 0.91 and an F1-score above 0.84, with withdrawn semesters, second-term credit load, academic probation history and mathematics and physics performance the strongest predictors. The authors applied SHAP analysis to make the model's predictions interpretable at both the whole-population and individual-student level, and note the system needs no external surveys or learning-management-system data, only data already held by the registrar.

Why it matters here: PASS can test the same combination the Sharjah team used, routine student-system records plus SHAP explainability, as a benchmark against models trained on anonymised Wits School of Education data, and borrow its use of withdrawn semesters and credit load as predictors that a Business Intelligence Services dataset is likely to hold too.

Al Hashmi, Zervopoulos, Elmehdi and Ozturk, Emerging Science Journal, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Aix-Marseille's own teacher-training institute launches a plurilingualism-and-AI exchange with Dakar's teacher training centre (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Aix-Marseille Université's INSPE and the Centre Régional de Formation des Personnels de l'Éducation (CRFPE) of Dakar launched a teaching and teacher-training cooperation project on 14 November 2025, supported by the French Embassy in Senegal. The launch set up two collaborative workspaces in Senegal, one on plurilingualism and artificial intelligence and one on fablab and artificial intelligence, to share experiences and co-construct teaching resources suited to local contexts. In March 2026 ten student teachers from the Dakar CRFPE are due to visit the Aix-Marseille INSPE to take courses and meet primary school pupils.

Why it matters here: Aix-Marseille's INSPE is the lead partner in the Erasmus+ KA171-HED project with Wits, and this Dakar exchange shows the same institute already running a bilingual, AI-themed teacher-training partnership with a Global South partner, a tested workspace format and a direct institutional contact for lessons on plurilingual content and for twinning the Wits mobility cohorts with a comparable Francophone West African partner.

Aix-Marseille Université, INSPE · Institutional programme page, Aix-Marseille Université INSPE (official partner institution), reporting the project's launch

entry.title: A smartphone's journey as a quiz game: a Horizon Europe critical raw materials game built with a Zambian partner university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
AGEMERA, a three-year Horizon Europe project coordinated by the University of Oulu in Finland with the University of Zambia among its 19 partners across 11 countries, published a free online serious game on critical raw materials. Modelled on the 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?' quiz format, the 20-question game follows a smartphone through extraction, processing, manufacturing, use and recycling, and is offered in several languages including Finnish, English, German, Spanish, Estonian and Romanian, as part of a wider educational package aimed at schools and universities. The project also mapped roughly 4,700 square kilometres of ground for critical raw materials across six EU states and Zambia.

Why it matters here: AGEMERA shows how a mining and metals supply chain, the raw material end of the structure-property chain the Wits study teaches, can be turned into a simple, freely reusable quiz game with a named African university as a genuine research partner rather than just a study site; its multi-language, schools-and-universities educational package is a workable model for the Wits team's own materials beyond the laboratory.

Joutsenvaara, University of Oulu Kerttu Saalasti Institute Blog, 2025 · Institutional blog post and project webpage from a Horizon Europe-funded research project, freely accessible online, not independently peer-reviewed

entry.title: Two advising algorithms built on the same state community college system send fewer at-risk Black students the extra help they need (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Virginia examined two prediction models, one for course completion and one for degree completion, built on system-wide administrative records from the Virginia Community College System covering 2007 to 2019. They found that if either model were used to target extra support at "at-risk" students, algorithmic bias would mean fewer marginal Black students received that support than White students, and that the size of the bias changed depending on whether "at-risk" was defined as the bottom decile or the bottom half of predicted scores. They trace part of the bias to the administrative data being less predictive of Black students' success than of White students' success, particularly for new students, and suggest that collecting more data could narrow the gap.

Why it matters here: A direct warning for PASS before any model goes near the University's Business Intelligence Services data: reporting one overall accuracy figure is not enough, the same model can send support to fewer at-risk Black or minoritised students depending only on how "at-risk" is defined, and the fix may be collecting more predictive data on under-served groups rather than adjusting the algorithm after the fact.

Bird, Castleman and Song, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (subscription access, Wiley)

entry.title: A simple decision tree built from two years of enrolment records flags dropout risk at a Malaysian private university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universiti Utara Malaysia, working with Oman's Ministry of Education, extracted 7,706 student records from a Malaysian private university's database covering the 2018 to 2019 intake to test decision tree and logistic regression classifiers for predicting dropout. After testing several data partitions, decision tree variants and logistic regression imputation methods, they found a chi-square decision tree with two branches performed best, reaching 89.49 percent accuracy on an 80/20 train-test split, and the chosen model also identified the variables most useful for predicting dropout. The authors frame dropout as a threat to university enrolment, revenue and student wellbeing, and argue the model could help flag at-risk students early.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable scale and data type to PASS's own starting point: a single institution's own enrolment records, modest classifiers rather than deep learning, and a result, 89.49 percent accuracy from a simple decision tree, that sets a realistic early benchmark for what anonymised Wits School of Education data alone might achieve before Business Intelligence Services data is added.

Roslan, Mohd Jamil, Mohd Shaharanee and Sultan Alawi, Journal of Advanced Research in Applied Sciences and Engineering Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC 4.0)

entry.title: Parma's Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund gives extreme priority to the most disadvantaged staff and students from Rwanda, Senegal and Niger (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The University of Parma's Centre for International University Cooperation (CUCI) was awarded an Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund supporting academic mobility with universities in Rwanda, Senegal and Niger. The fund covers 21 incoming teaching-staff positions, who take three-week laboratory training courses and summer schools updating pedagogical methods, and 19 incoming student places for three to four month internships. Selection explicitly requires gender balance and gives extreme priority to the most economically disadvantaged students and teaching staff from the partner countries.

Why it matters here: This KA171-HED consortium shows a concrete, publicly stated equity rule, explicit gender balance and extreme priority for the most disadvantaged applicants, for selecting incoming teaching staff and structuring their pedagogical training, a model the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership could adapt when it sets its own selection criteria for master's, doctoral and staff mobility cohorts.
